BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Near to slightly below normal temperatures are expected to remain in place throughout the long-term period as active patterns continue.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Second low pressure system returning rain and mountain snow Sunday through Monday.
- Cooler and unsettled pattern continuing next week with snow levels potentially lowering to valley floors by the end of the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: As the active low pressure system steers eastward out of our area, Saturday will see remnant showers and light mountain snow taper off over the west-central ID mountains and Magic Valley through the afternoon. An upper level ridge will begin building overhead on Saturday with partly to mostly sunny skies. Saturday will be 10-15 degrees cooler in most areas, but still several degrees above normal. The dry break will continue through late Saturday, before the next Pacific trough system approaches the area with showers developing in eastern OR by Sunday morning.

Except for eastern OR coming under the trough's arrival, most areas will be dry and 5-10 degrees warmer than normal on Sunday. A slow-moving band of precipitation will gradually steer eastward across eastern OR, before reaching southwest Idaho by late Sunday evening into Monday morning. This system will slowly trek across southwest ID throughout Monday, returning valley rain showers and light mountain snow showers. Valleys will generally see relatively lighter rain accumulations at around 0.25 inches total. High terrain areas over the central ID mountains and the ID/NV border will see the bulk of precipitation from this system on Monday. Snow levels will mostly hang in the 5500-7000 ft MSL range through most of Monday, before gradually dropping down into the 4500-5500 ft range by late Monday. As such, minor snow accumulations of around 1 inches are likely over the central ID mountains and ID/NV border through late Monday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The upper-level trough digging across our area through Tuesday will return a cooling pattern for the remainder of the week. Valley rain and mountain snow showers will continue on the southwest ID side through Tuesday morning as it tapers off east by the afternoon. Snow levels will drop to 4500-5500 feet by Tuesday morning. This will bring minor snow accumulation to the Central Idaho Mountains and the Idaho-Nevada border, with Tuesday night snowfall totals between 1 to 3 inches. A ridge of high pressure will briefly build into the region on Wednesday, bringing mostly dry conditions.

Near to slightly below normal temperatures are expected to remain in place throughout the long-term period as active patterns continue. There is generally strong guidance agreement on a deep Pacific upper low digging into the Pacific Northwest and Great Basin regions Wednesday through Friday. There is still slight guidance uncertainty over the upper low's exact movement pattern going into Friday, but a 50-80% chance of precipitation remains for Wednesday through Friday. This active troughing pattern will bring a further cooldown. Considerable guidance uncertainty remains for snow level trends from midweek to the end of the week. There is potential for snow levels to drop down to valley floors Wednesday through Friday, bringing the possibility of light snow showers over valleys. For now, the current long-range forecast has rain and/or rain/snow mix staying the dominant precipitation type for most lower elevation valleys through Friday. The low pressure system will steer eastward out of the region by early Saturday, with an amplifying Pacific ridge building immediately behind it. Saturday will see partly clearing skies and drier conditions.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: A shortwave trough is still on track to bring mountain snow on Wednesday with the Denver metro and east CO plains remaining dry.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Cloudy and cooler today with areas fog this morning across northeast Colorado.
- Scattered rain and mountain snow showers, mainly south of I-70.
- A return to mild and dry conditions Sunday through Tuesday.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: The recent high-resolution model runs have trended closer to global models, showing the best lift and moisture staying south of I-70 through this evening. Lowered PoPs and precipitation amounts north of I-70 due to this. Most models are dry, but a few show light precipitation (less than a tenth inch). Fog is spreading across northeast Colorado as expected. Webcams and observations so far show only a couple spots where visibility is a quarter mile or less. Will hold off for now on issuing a Dense Fog Advisory, but will continue to monitor.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: No major changes have been made to the previous forecast. Fog is still expected to spread west later tonight and into Saturday morning as low level moisture gets wrapped around a surface low north of Denver. The fog could be dense at times, lowering visibilities to less than 1/4 mile over Denver, the I-25 corridor, parts of Lincoln County, and the surrounding plains. The fog is less likely to reach the higher terrain of the Palmer Divide and if it does, it should be more patchy and shorter-lived.

A shortwave trough will bring a surge of mid level moisture to much of the state on Saturday which will help promote mountain snow in afternoon and evening. Flow at the 700mb level will be west to northwest, favoring orographic lift for the central mountains and the highest peaks of the Park Range. Model soundings sampled over various mountain ranges in our area show relatively deep moist profiles with saturation along the dendritic growth zone. However, given the weak state of the shortwave as it slides over our area and lackluster synoptic forcing for ascent, snowfall is expected to be light orographic in nature. Accumulations in the 1 to 3 inch range will be possible for elevations above 10kft, with locally higher amounts above 12kt. Mountain valleys could also see some snow showers throughout the afternoon, but no accumulation is expected given the marginal surface and air temperatures (highs in the 40s). For the Denver metro and east CO plains, fog may be slow to erode and scattered low clouds could persist through early afternoon. Despite the abundant moisture at the lowest levels of the atmosphere, model soundings for Denver show a stubborn dry layer at around the 700mb level. Any showers that try to develop over the Denver area will initially struggle to reach the ground so we have limited the better PoPs (17%-40%) to the late afternoon and overnight hours. If showers are able to linger into the early morning hours of Sunday (~30% chance), a few snowflakes to even a light dusting of snow cannot be ruled out over the crest of the Palmer Divide. Otherwise, patchy fog will be possible once again Sunday morning over the parts of the Denver metro and CO plains.

Conditions dry out state-wide on Sunday afternoon as an upper level ridge begins to build over the Four Corners. This ridge will warm temperatures back up to well above average for the season Monday through Tuesday, with afternoon highs in the low 60s for the plains, and 50s at the mountain valleys. Tuesday afternoon could be breezy as the pressure gradient tightens ahead of the next system and higher wind speeds aloft from the jet positioned over the area mix down to the surface.

A shortwave trough is still on track to bring mountain snow on Wednesday with the Denver metro and east CO plains remaining dry. While there is still quite a bit of uncertainty with this system, at least a couple of inches of snow accumulation seem reasonable for the central and northern mountains. Beyond Wednesday, model ensembles and deterministic runs show fundamental differences with every run cycle. Perhaps the only "change" has been a slight trend towards cooler solutions that bring a cutoff low to the Four Corners region sometime late next week. At this time, ~40% of the NBM members show at least one inch of snow for Denver within a 72 hour period. There is also little to no agreement in the timing of this system, with some solutions bringing the cutoff low into the area as early as Friday morning, while others push this system back to Tuesday of Thanksgiving week. What we do know at this time is that temperatures in long-range ensembles keep trending at or below average for the long term (days 8-15), increasing our confidence in a colder end to November.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Friday...For climatology enthusiast, November 20th is the latest first measurable snowfall event in recorded history for Cheyenne, with at least one tenth of an inch of snow measured on the ground.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Chances of precipitation increase over the weekend for the mountains, with a few spotty showers possible mainly along and south of the I-80 corridor.
- A more active pattern is expected into the middle of next week, with precipitation chances returning Wednesday into Thursday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Surface observations and 10.3-3.9 um IR Satellite loop shows another round of low clouds and areas of fog early this morning, this time with higher areal coverage compared to last night. Fog and lower visibility seems to be more confined near the I-25 corridor on the lee-side of the Laramie Range, and across the Cheyenne Ridge extending into Kimball Nebraska. Dense fog has been brief and limited to the lower valleys, but will continue to monitor the areal extent as we head into the early morning hours in the event we need a Dense Fog Advisory. Otherwise, not many changes to the weekend forecast as the next Pacific storm system, currently moving eastward over the Great Basin Region, is expected to stay south of the Wyoming/Colorado border today. In fact, models have trended even further south with this system as of the 00z model runs with high res ensembles (REFS) and the HRRR showing hardly any precipitation at all outside the mountains today and this evening. Given this trend, decreased POP a bit along the I-80 corridor with POP near 50 percent across the mountains for maybe an inch or two of snow above 9000 feet. Cooler today with ample cloud cover and upslope south to southeast winds. Highs will struggle to reach the 50s and will generally top out in the mid 40s to mid 50s through this afternoon. There is some uncertainty with today's high temperatures as low clouds and even some patchy fog may linger into the afternoon hours. This may keep high temperatures in the low 40s for a few places across far eastern Wyoming and western Nebraska. Also, low clouds and fog may return to the high plains, after a brief break, later tonight. Fog is expected to be more patchy compared to the last few days with breezy winds near the surface.

For Sunday, models show the Great Basin storm system ejecting south and east into Texas and Oklahoma by Sunday morning. Lingering morning cloud cover should give way to mostly sunny skies by noon-ish with high temperatures trending back into the 50s to low 60s. Shortwave ridge axis will translate eastward into the Intermountain West and northern Front Range by later on Sunday with a gradual warming trend likely into Monday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Monday...The unusually mild weather continues with broad southwest flow aloft, and high 500 mb heights near 5760 meters overhead. This will induce decent surface lee troughing and mild weather enthusiasts will rejoice with 700 mb temperatures near 6 Celsius and downslope warming boosting maximum temperatures into the mid 50s to mid 60s.

Tuesday...Stronger southwest flow aloft develops across our neck of the woods here in southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska, with a slightly negatively tilted shortwave trough aloft moving across Idaho, Utah and western Wyoming, with surface lee troughing keeping our weather conditions high and dry once again with slightly cooler 700 mb temperatures near 4 Celsius and slightly cooler temperatures for our forecast area, though still on the mild side.

Wednesday...The aforementioned shortwave trough aloft loses amplitude as it moves to eastern Montana and the western Dakotas by sunrise, sending its associated cold front into our counties, Pacific originated. As is typical with these systems, will see scattered to numerous rain and snow showers early in the day west of a Douglas to Laramie line due to dynamics and orographics with some decent snows across our northern Laramie, Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges, though downslope wind east of the mountains and Laramie Range will as usual provide a rain shadow effect with little if any precipitation east of the Interstate 25 corridor and Laramie Range. Orographic snows will continue in the afternoon for our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges, and we may need some type of Winter Weather Highlight such as a Winter Weather Advisory, if model congruency continues.

Thursday...Looks like a windy and relatively mild day for November, the beginning of our typical windy November through March windy season. Strong southwest flow aloft continues, and our wind prone locations such as Arlington, Bordeaux and the Interstate 80 Summit between Laramie and Cheyenne may see some strong winds, and possible wind highlights.

Friday...For climatology enthusiast, November 20th is the latest first measurable snowfall event in recorded history for Cheyenne, with at least one tenth of an inch of snow measured on the ground. Interestingly, this coincides with a decent and progressive neutrally tilted shortwave trough aloft that is progged to move across our forecast area with a rather strong cold frontal passage, which if model timing is correct will produce decent orographic snows for our Laramie, Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges, and some likely accumulating snow for lower elevations due to the thickness packing along the front, dynamics and synoptic forcing, especially if the track of the system is a bit further south across Colorado, rather than over Wyoming as currently depicted, so please stay tuned to the latest forecasts from your entire National Weather Service team. In any event. Friday the 20th, will be a cold and blustery day with measurable snow becoming increasingly likely at many locations, although snowfall amounts are quite unpredictable for day 7, one week out. Maximum temperatures will only be in the upper 30s to upper 40s with breezy to windy conditions, only six days before Thanksgiving.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: The H500 hand analysis map this evening is playing out as expected with an Omega-like pattern in place. A strong downstream blocking trough over eastern NOAM is forcing the upstream trough to negatively tilt as it moves farther inland.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Valley rain and mountain snow returns to the forecast this weekend favoring the southern mountains and adjacent foothills.
- Quiet conditions return briefly Sunday afternoon and Monday before another round of precipitation arrives during the middle of next week.
- Unsettled and cool conditions are favored to persist into the late week period as well.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The H500 hand analysis map this evening is playing out as expected with an Omega-like pattern in place. A strong downstream blocking trough over eastern NOAM is forcing the upstream trough to negatively tilt as it moves farther inland. In between the highly amplified ridge remains but has shifted onto the Plains from 24 hours ago. Showers have developed in the western CWA and with a strong PV lobe rotating across the 4 Corners overnight...a few strikes of lightning will be possible. Weaker echos on the radar suggest moisture is increasing on the southerly flow into the southern mountains but so far webcams and snotels are relatively quiet. This will be changing in the next few hours with the heaviest precipitation still expected during the early to mid morning hours on Saturday as the surface front and large scale coincide with moisture in place. Snow levels still look to hover in the 8-9kft level for the bulk of this event...lowering to mountain bases by sunset tomorrow as the system is exiting. The southern mountains...especially the crescent of the southern San Juans remain favored to catch the best moisture and produce the highest snow amounts. 4 to 8 inches should cover most of the advisory area though hi-res guidance is picking out some of the favored high peaks and snotels for the higher amounts closer to a foot. Otherwise 1 to 4 inches should cover the remaining mountain forecasts though colder northwest flow often throws some bonus inches. QPF amounts in the southern basins are still in the 1/3 to 2/3 inch range for liquid precipitation with again some isolated higher amounts possible due to the convection. Hydrographs are still only showing some minor rises on the smaller tributaries to the San Juan with the main steam holding steady. Temperatures will be much cooler tomorrow in the post frontal environment but overall end up near to above normal in the drier northern CWA and 5 to 10 degrees cooler in the wetter southern areas. By sunrise on Sunday the trough and PV stream will be east of the divide and ridging will be translate across the Great Basin to the Great Plains through Monday afternoon as the next deep trough arrives to the West. Models still show a moderate AR with this system which again survives the upstream terrain and brings more widespread precipitation to the area in the mid week time frame. The QG forcing has been trending a bit farther North which will bring better chances for precipitation to our northern CWA which as been missing out lately. This system is a tad cooler and this should translate to better a snowfall forecast for most of the higher terrain...but will need to continue to watch trends in speed and track as we get nearer. Temperatures will moderate to near normal Monday into Tuesday before a colder end to the week. Models spread still significant and changing daily on how the pattern in the late week period evolves but the overall flavor is for a large trough in the West keeping unsettled conditions on the radar.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Deeper upper trough then moves into the western U.S. late week, before ejecting eastward through the Rockies and into the plains late Fri into Sat.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Upper trough crosses southern Colorado today, with a couple waves of showers/isolated t-storms moving through the area in the afternoon/evening.

- Higher mountains, above 8-9k feet, will see snow today, heaviest in the eastern San Juan Mts, where 4-7 inches is expected. Rain/snow mix possible Monument Hill late this evening, though any accumulations here will be minor.
- Dry with a slow warning trend Sun-Mon, before another fast moving trough brings snow to the mountains, mainly along the Continental Divide Tue/Wed.

- A strong winter storm will move through the Rockies and onto the plains toward next weekend, though much uncertainty remains on the ultimate track of the system and where the greatest impacts/heaviest precip will occur.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: Updated to add fog to El Paso and Pueblo Counties through the early morning. Area webcams and observations are indicating visibilities falling to 1 to 2 miles. A few locations could see denser fog through morning.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Upper trough over the wrn U.S. early this morning will move across Colorado today into this evening, before closing off a weak upper low across the southern plains early Sunday morning. Already seeing some light snow over the San Juans as of midnight, and expect snow here to become heavier/steadier overnight into early Sat morning as upward motion increases. A few rain/mountain snow showers will spread farther east over most of the high terrain/interior valleys toward sunrise, then a couple waves of showers will develop and move through the mountains and across the plains today, especially this afternoon and evening. May even be enough instability for a few t-storms over the eastern mountains and plains, especially late afternoon into the evening as colder air aloft moves across and lapse rates steepen. Bulk of the precip should be done by midnight, with just some lingering showers and patchy fog into early Sunday morning, mainly on the plains. In general, forecast precip amounts have continued to trend downward, with one or two tenths of an inch of liquid at most locations. Exceptions will be the higher elevations of the San Juans, where a quarter to half inch of liquid (snowfall of 3-7 inches) is possible, with perhaps the higher peaks of the Sangres seeing a quarter inch (2-4 inches of snow). If we do see some stronger convection on the plains, a quick quarter to half inch of rain is possible in isolated spots, with a few CAMs (RRFS/HRRR) occasionally hinting at this. Clouds will keep temps cool today, with highs mainly in the 30s/40s, though a few spots along I-25 could reach the low 50s if we see a few breaks in the clouds midday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Clouds and cool temps will linger Sunday on the plains, as Srn Plains upper low is slow to move eastward, while mountains and interior valleys see more sun and slightly warmer temps. Dry and warmer all areas on Mon, as upper ridge moves across and low/mid level flow turns more swly. Next upper wave moves though late Tue into Wed, though system continues to look rather progressive/fast moving, which will likely limit precip amounts over srn CO. As wave approaches, lee surface trough on the plains will promote deep mixing and warmer temperatures both Tue and Wed, with readings in the 60s along and east of I-25, and potentially approaching 70f at a few locations across the lower Arkansas Valley. Mountains, especially along the Continental Divide, will see a quick shot of snow Tue night/Wed morning, before precip ends by late day Wed as wave moves east. Suspect we'll see accumulating snow and perhaps some brief travel issues over the higher mountain passes, though not looking at major impacts at this point.

Deeper upper trough then moves into the western U.S. late week, before ejecting eastward through the Rockies and into the plains late Fri into Sat. System has potential to be impactful with deep surface low spinning up over the High Plains and strong winds/heavy snow developing, though many questions remain concerning the ultimate track of the system and the location of the heaviest precip. Model trends have been slowly shifting northward the past 24 hrs or so, with surface low spinning up slightly too far north to bring heavy snow to srn CO, though quick look at 14/00z ECMWF deterministic model shows it could be close. Still rather far out of get an exact track at this point, but system needs to be monitored as it won't take much of a southerly shift to bring heavy snow/wind to srn CO.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: As this trough exits the area, it will be followed quickly by yet another storm system.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Valley rain and mountain snow will continue through the morning, before shifting to a more showery nature this afternoon and gradually ending.
- The heaviest snow accumulations will occur across the southern mountains, where a winter weather advisory continues through 11 AM this morning.

- Another colder storm will impact the region Monday evening through Wednesday morning, bringing snow levels as low as 4800 feet to northern Utah. This storm will bring more substantial snow accumulations to the mountains of Utah, with another 6 to 12 inches of snow increasing in probability for the upper Cottonwoods, as well as the southern mountains.

- Another even colder system will impact much of Utah Thursday into Saturday. This storm has the highest probability of snow levels down to valley floors (around 60% chance of snow levels at or below 4200 ft by Saturday morning). Current forecast for valley floors is up to an inch of snow.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A negatively-tilted trough is making its way across the western CONUS this evening. This trough is the result of phasing between a southern stream system ejecting across the desert southwest and a larger system over the PacNW coast. Southerly flow ahead of the trough axis (which currently extends from the Washington coast through western Arizona) remains in place over Utah this evening, which has drawn moisture northward into the forecast area. Showers have already developed, and will continue to increase in coverage overnight. These showers occurring in the warm sector will maintain snow levels mainly above 8 kft through much of the night.

A cold front is expected to move into western Utah before 12z and reach the I-15 corridor between 15-17z. Widespread precipitation near the cold front is then expected to quickly decrease behind it, clearing out in many valleys through the late morning and early afternoon timeframe. The exception will be the mountains and immediate upslope areas where a brief period of favorable orographics will maintain precipitation, especially along northwest aspects. Additionally, some enhancement off the GSL may allow additional showers along the central Wasatch Front and adjacent mountains into the afternoon. Snow levels will quickly lower with the passage of the cold front, with H7 temperatures falling to -4 to -5C towards the end of the precipitation event. This would suggest snow levels down to 6.5-7 kft, although the greatest (and any real impactful) accumulation can be expected above 8-9 kft. Most valleys are expected to see between 0.25-0.7 inches of precipitation with this storm, with between 0.4 to 1.25 inches in the mountains. Locally higher amounts are possible especially near Brian Head and in the upper Cottonwoods. Snow amounts are generally expected to be in the 4-8 inch range (especially above 8-9 kft) with higher amounts in the upper Cottonwoods and near Brian Head.

An upper ridge shifting into the area Saturday night through Sunday will bring a period of drier and stable conditions. The ridge will shift east for Monday, bringing increased southerly flow ahead of the next approaching storm system. This progressive pattern will keep any strong inversions at bay.

The next storm looks to arrive over Utah late Monday night or Tuesday, impacting the area into Wednesday morning. Latest model trends suggest another quick-hitting progressive trough which will bring another round of widespread precipitation to the area. However, this storm looks to be associated with a somewhat cooler airmass. LREF means of H7 temperatures for portions of northern Utah dip as low as -8C, which suggest snow levels down to at least 5 kft.

As this trough exits the area, it will be followed quickly by yet another storm system. While cluster analysis of global ensembles show high confidence in a storm for the second half of next week, there remain some differences regarding its timing and evolution. This storm may arrive as early as Wednesday night but may hold off until later Thursday. Additionally, some members are suggesting that this will end up being another progressive trough while others maintain a closed low solution which would bring an extended period of precipitation to the area. Latest cluster analysis shows an approximately 55%/45% split, favoring the closed low solution slightly.

2660.travel_advice: Dangerous avalanche conditions. Careful snowpack evaluation, cautious route-finding and conservative decision-making essential.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: Avalanche danger will increase throughout the day on Saturday as new snow accumulates. The most dangerous slopes will be shady, high-elevation areas where over a foot of fresh snow forms a slab over an existing weak layer. In these places, you could trigger an avalanche large enough to bury you.

Watch for cracking or collapsing in the new snow, as these are clear warning signs that a slab has formed. Safer travel conditions can be found on lower-angled slopes, at lower elevations, or where you find less than a foot of new snow.

2658.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: Danger increases on Saturday as new snowfall lands on weak old snow surfaces. The most dangerous areas will be where winds drift new snow into thicker and stiffer slabs on lee slopes facing northwest to northeast through east. If you find more than 8 inches of drifted snow on steep slopes above treeline, you could trigger a small avalanche that could wipe you off your feet.

Watch for cracking or collapsing in the new snow, as these are clear warning signs that a slab has formed. Safer travel conditions can be found on lower-angled slopes, at lower elevations, or in wind-sheltered terrain.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: A few inches of new snow late on Sturday won't be enough to raise avalanche concerns. Most slopes don't have enough snow for avalanches and are safe for travel. At high elevations, steer around isolated spots of firm, drifted snow below ridges or in gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has yet to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. Except on the steepest, highest-elevation, north-facing slopes, the mountains are snow-free. Avalanches will be unlikely until a deeper, layered snowpack builds. Once winter does arrive, even a small amount of snow with enough wind can create unstable avalanche conditions. If you're traveling in the mountains during or after a storm, be wary of steep, wind-loaded features at upper elevations and watch out for terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information as more snow accumulates
hazard_discussion: Due to a warm and dry fall season, the mountains in our forecast zones remain mostly dry, with little to no snow on the ground. As you're waiting for winter to arrive and the mountain snowpack to stack up, here are a few things to consider:
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Jason Konigsberg
bottom_line: Avalanche conditions are generally safe. The weather forecast is calling for 2 to 4 inches of snow, which won't be enough to raise avalanche concerns. If you are at high elevations and observe more than about 6 inches of snow with wind drifting, and shooting cracks, steer around steep terrain features at these upper elevations.
